books.title: As Long as the Lemon Trees Grow
books.author: Zoulfa Katouh
books.ratingNote: Extremely high average ratings across Goodreads and retail sites; frequently cited as a standout contemporary YA novel.
reviewSummary: Set in war-torn Syria, the novel follows Salama, a pharmacy student turned hospital volunteer, as she struggles with grief, survivor’s guilt, and the impossible choice between fleeing and staying.
Readers describe the book as devastating yet deeply human, praising its refusal to romanticize war while still centering love, friendship, and resilience.
Many reviews highlight the tenderness of the romance and the haunting presence of Salama’s imagined companion, which reflects her fractured mental state.
Often recommended for readers who want emotionally intense, socially grounded YA that lingers long after finishing.
books.ageNote: 15+; includes war violence, death, and heavy emotional content.

books.title: Grown
books.author: Tiffany D. Jackson
books.ratingNote: Consistently rated in the mid-4s with strong critical and reader response.
reviewSummary: A psychological thriller inspired by real-life abuse cases, following a teenage girl navigating fame, manipulation, and trauma.
Readers praise Jackson’s unflinching look at grooming and power imbalances, especially in entertainment spaces.
The nonlinear structure and mounting dread are frequently cited as making the book impossible to put down.
Often recommended for discussions around consent, silence, and believing survivors.

books.title: Monday’s Not Coming
books.author: Tiffany D. Jackson
books.ratingNote: Highly rated with strong word-of-mouth among librarians and educators.
reviewSummary: Claudia searches for her missing best friend Monday while adults and institutions fail to take her concerns seriously.
Readers praise the fragmented timeline, which mirrors confusion, denial, and systemic neglect.
The reveal is frequently described as shocking and heartbreaking rather than sensational.
Often cited as a powerful critique of how missing Black girls are overlooked.

books.title: Let Me Hear a Rhyme
books.author: Tiffany D. Jackson
books.ratingNote: Strong ratings, particularly from readers interested in music-centered YA.
reviewSummary: Set in late-1990s Brooklyn, teens attempt to preserve their friend’s legacy after his death through hip-hop.
Praised for its authentic portrayal of grief, ambition, and Black youth culture.
Readers love the musical atmosphere and the complicated moral choices the characters face.
Frequently recommended for fans of stories where art becomes survival.

books.title: Hani and Ishu’s Guide to Fake Dating
books.author: Adiba Jaigirdar
books.ratingNote: Strong reader ratings, especially within queer YA spaces.
reviewSummary: A fake-dating romcom between two Bangladeshi Irish teens navigating school politics and family expectations.
Readers praise the balance of sweetness and realism, particularly around cultural pressure.
Often highlighted for joyful queer Muslim representation.
Recommended for fans of soft, character-driven romance.

books.title: You Should See Me in a Crown
books.author: Leah Johnson
reviewSummary: Liz Lighty runs for prom queen to secure scholarship money and discovers confidence and love along the way.
Praised for its joyful tone and lovable protagonist.
Readers appreciate the mix of humor, romance, and ambition.
Frequently recommended as a comfort read with substance.

books.title: This Is My America
books.author: Kim Johnson
books.ratingNote: Strong ratings and frequent classroom adoption.
reviewSummary: A teen investigates her father’s wrongful conviction on death row.
Readers praise the tightly paced plot and moral urgency.
Often described as anger-inducing but necessary.
Recommended for readers interested in justice and activism.

books.title: The Henna Wars
books.author: Adiba Jaigirdar
reviewSummary: A rivals-to-lovers story centered on cultural ownership and identity.
Readers appreciate the nuanced look at microaggressions.
Praised for queer Muslim representation.
Often recommended for contemporary school settings.

books.title: Jay’s Gay Agenda
books.author: Jason June
books.ratingNote: Very positive reception among queer YA readers.
reviewSummary: A funny, heartfelt story about a teen exploring identity after moving to Seattle.
Praised for sex-positive messaging without shame.
Readers enjoy the humor and found-family dynamics.
Often described as affirming and joyful.

books.title: Love from A to Z
books.author: S.K. Ali
reviewSummary: A journal-based romance between two Muslim teens dealing with illness and faith.
Praised for warmth, vulnerability, and representation.
Readers love the travel setting and emotional honesty.
A favorite for soft romance readers.

title: Letters to the Lost
author: Brigid Kemmerer
ratingNote: Strong, consistent ratings across Goodreads and retail platforms.
reviewSummary: Juliet pours her grief into letters written to her deceased mother, never expecting someone anonymous to write back and slowly become essential to her healing.
Readers praise the emotional vulnerability of the letter format, which allows both protagonists to reveal themselves gradually and honestly.
The story balances romance with genuine processing of loss, avoiding the trap of love magically fixing grief.
Often recommended for readers who enjoy intimate, emotionally grounded romances.
ageNote: 13+; grief, emotional distress, and mild romance.

title: Call It What You Want
author: Brigid Kemmerer
ratingNote: Average ratings sit in the low 4s with a strong teen readership.
reviewSummary: After public scandals ruin their families, two teens find refuge in anonymity, music, and each other.
Readers highlight how accurately the novel captures social fallout, gossip culture, and isolation.
The romance is praised for being quiet, slow, and built on mutual understanding rather than drama.
Frequently described as emotionally heavy but comforting.

title: Long Story Short
author: Serena Kaylor
ratingNote: Positive early reception with ratings clustering just above 4 stars.
reviewSummary: A summer road trip forces siblings to confront old wounds, family secrets, and unresolved grief.
Readers appreciate the realistic sibling dynamics—messy, sarcastic, and deeply loving.
The pacing is often described as gentle and reflective rather than plot-heavy.
Recommended for fans of character-driven contemporary stories.

title: Tokyo Ever After
author: Emiko Jean
ratingNote: Consistently rated around the low 4s with broad appeal.
reviewSummary: Izumi discovers she’s the lost princess of Japan and must navigate palace life, cultural expectations, and her own identity.
Readers love the mix of fish-out-of-water humor and emotional depth.
Praised for exploring diaspora identity and belonging without glamorizing royalty.
Often compared to a modern YA Princess Diaries with more cultural nuance.

title: We Are the Perfect Girl
author: Ami Polonsky
ratingNote: Strong reception from readers interested in mental health representation.
reviewSummary: A boarding-school mystery centered on a girl questioning both her environment and her own perception.
Readers praise the atmospheric tension and slow-building unease.
Mental health themes are treated with ambiguity rather than neat answers.
Recommended for readers who enjoy psychological contemporary novels.

title: If I Tell You the Truth
author: Jasmin Kaur
ratingNote: Generally rated around 4 stars with strong poetic appeal.
reviewSummary: A verse novel about a girl caught between cultural expectations, secrecy, and her need for autonomy.
Readers highlight the lyrical language and emotional clarity of the poetry.
Often praised for South Asian representation and exploration of silence.
Recommended for fans of poetry-forward YA.

title: If I Could Go Back
author: Brianna Bourne
reviewSummary: A time-loop story exploring regret, accountability, and emotional growth.
Readers appreciate the balance between speculative elements and grounded character work.
Often described as introspective rather than action-driven.
Recommended for readers who like quiet what-if narratives.

title: House Party
author: Eric Rosswood
reviewSummary: A single-night story centered around a chaotic party and intersecting teen lives.
Readers enjoy the fast pacing and ensemble cast.
Themes of accountability and peer pressure resonate strongly.
Often recommended as a quick, high-energy read.

title: Hungry Hearts
author: Elsie Chapman & Caroline Tung Richmond
reviewSummary: A collection of interconnected short stories centered around food and love.
Readers praise the diversity of voices and cultural settings.
The anthology format makes it easy to dip in and out.
Recommended for readers who enjoy slice-of-life storytelling.

title: Why We Fly
author: Kimberly Jones & Gilly Segal
ratingNote: Generally positive reception from sports-fiction readers.
reviewSummary: Two girls bond through track while navigating racial tension and grief.
Readers praise the depiction of female friendship and athletic discipline.
The novel balances competition with emotional vulnerability.
Often recommended for readers interested in sports-centered YA.

title: Rani Choudhury Must Die
author: Adiba Jaigirdar
ratingNote: Average ratings cluster just under 4 stars with strong niche appeal.
reviewSummary: A sharp, witty rivals-to-lovers story following two academically competitive teens forced to work together.
Readers enjoy the banter-heavy dialogue and the way academic pressure is portrayed as both motivating and suffocating.
Praised for South Asian Muslim representation and humor that doesn’t undercut emotional stakes.
Often recommended for readers who like smart, fast-paced contemporary romance.

title: Salt the Water
author: Candice Iloh
ratingNote: Generally rated just under 4 stars; appreciated for its emotional honesty.
reviewSummary: Follows three teens coping with grief after a classmate’s death, each from a different perspective.
Readers praise the nonlinear structure and poetic language that mirrors emotional disorientation.
Often highlighted for centering Black grief without sensationalizing tragedy.
Recommended for readers who like literary, introspective YA.

title: Beast Rider
author: Tony Johnston
ratingNote: Moderate ratings with particular praise for its subject matter.
reviewSummary: A survival story following a boy fleeing cartel violence across the U.S.–Mexico border.
Readers commend the tense pacing and unflinching look at displacement and fear.
Often recommended alongside other migration-focused YA novels.
Praised for highlighting human resilience under extreme circumstances.

title: Technically, You Started It
author: Lana Wood Johnson
ratingNote: Average ratings sit in the high 3s with a strong teen readership.
reviewSummary: Two teens bond through anonymous messaging, unaware they’re rivals in real life.
Readers enjoy the modern epistolary format and realistic social-media dynamics.
The romance is praised for being playful but emotionally sincere.
Recommended for fans of texting-based contemporary stories.

title: The Me I Meant to Be
author: Sophie Gonzales
ratingNote: Generally positive reception within queer YA readership.
reviewSummary: A teen grapples with public scandal and the pressure to redefine himself.
Readers praise the honest exploration of masculinity, accountability, and growth.
The story avoids easy redemption, which many find refreshing.
Often recommended for readers who want emotionally challenging contemporary YA.

title: The Marvelous Mirza Girls
author: Sheba Karim
ratingNote: Lower average ratings but strong appreciation from readers seeking family-centered stories.
reviewSummary: Three sisters reunite at their parents’ Wisconsin motel during a tense family transition.
Readers appreciate the realistic sibling dynamics—supportive, resentful, and loving all at once.
Praised for Muslim American representation and emotional nuance.
Often recommended for readers who enjoy quiet, family-focused narratives.
